title: architecture-first-platform-cto-playbook-and-case-summaries-2026
author: Nina Park
body:
Summary

This playbook is targeted at platform architects, CTOs, and senior infra engineers evaluating inference platforms for production at scale. It combines an architecture-first positioning narrative, a competitive brief focused on operational tradeoffs, a compact pitch-deck outline tuned for technical boards, practical pricing guidance with worked examples, two short customer case summaries, and a focused Security FAQ prospects typically ask us. Use this doc during technical discovery calls, executive briefings, and commercial proposal reviews.

TL;DR (one-liner value props)

- Predictable latency and unit economics across hosted, dedicated, and private modes.
- Deployment parity: same API and rollout primitives across clouds, on-prem, and VPCs.
- Cost controls that map directly to engineering levers: batching, kv/prefix cache, and quantization profiles.

Why architecture-first matters to platform teams

Platform teams own uptime, privacy, and long-term cost. They evaluate vendors against three broad vectors:

1) Operational predictability (SLOs, fallbacks, tracing)
2) Integration friction (VPC, KMS, SIEM / audit logs, rollout semantics)
3) Unit economics and control (per-token cost, burst behavior, reserved capacity)

This playbook aligns Redwood’s messaging to those vectors and gives concrete scripts, metrics, and decision aids.

Positioning and message map (audience-tailored)

- Platform/Infra lead (what to emphasize):
  - Deterministic latency guarantees (p95 < 220 ms for 512-token Gen on Dedicated small pool) and SLA-backed uptime (99.9% regional for Dedicated).
  - Predictable autoscaling that preserves cache locality and KV reuse.
  - Integration checklist: VPC peering, single-tenant control plane option, HSM/KMS key management, and per-route audit logs.

- Security/compliance lead (what to emphasize):
  - Private deployment mode with customer-managed control plane, retention controls, and HSM integration for key material.
  - Audit evidence: request/response hash retention at 30/90/365d retention tiers and SOC2-style access logs.

- Product/Platform PM (what to emphasize):
  - Cost modeling knobs tied to product SLAs (e.g., aggressive batching for background jobs, low-latency pools for user-facing flows).
  - Canary and A/B rollout primitives that let you pin model versions and failover gracefully.

Competitive brief (operational focus)

Competitors compared at the architecture level:

1) Public LLM APIs (OpenAI-equivalent)
  - Strengths: simplest integration, broad model catalog, managed model upgrades.
  - Weaknesses: limited control over routing, variable latency under load, less transparent unit economics and few on-prem options.
  - Win guidance: emphasize need for deterministic SLAs and data residency.

2) Cloud-managed GPU endpoints (AWS/GCP equivalents)
  - Strengths: integrated infra and billing, broad ecosystem.
  - Weaknesses: customers bear runtime tuning, KV cache/shard complexity, and often build significant control plane glue.
  - Win guidance: focus on out-of-box inference optimizations (continuous batching, KV cache) and SRE time saved.

3) Inference runtime vendors/self-hosted stacks (ScaleRuntime/WarpServe analogs)
  - Strengths: deep control and cost at peak scale.
  - Weaknesses: heavy ops burden, lifecycle management, model onboarding friction.
  - Win guidance: highlight Redwood’s hybrid model (hosted + private) and our model onboarding playbook that shortens time-to-safe-serve.

Decision heuristics for prospects (simple checklist)

- If you need sub-250ms p95 for user-facing flows and SLA-backed uptime: prioritize Dedicated or Private.
- If you must keep full control of keys and network: require Private with customer-managed control plane and HSM.
- If your primary objective is to minimize engineering headcount for inference ops: choose Hosted API with reserved capacity.

Pitch deck outline (recommended 8–12 slides for technical board)

1) Title: Deal name, prospect org, and one-line outcome (e.g., "Reduce inference cost by 42% while improving p95 latency for chat flows").
2) Context: scale, workloads (concurrent QPS, average request size, percent user-facing).
3) Core value props: predictable economics, deployment parity, and operational controls.
4) Architecture diagram: show request flow, model catalog, routing policies, fallback tiers, and KV cache.
5) SLOs and observability: p50/p95/p99 expectations, token-level cost breakdowns, tracing hooks.
6) Pricing starters: hosted per-token bands, reserved capacity commitments, and private licensing.
7) Migration/rollout plan: pilot -> canary -> global rollout (with timelines).
8) Security & compliance: network, keys, audit logs, and evidence items.
9) Case snapshot: 2-3 slides of customer examples tied to the prospect’s vertical.
10) Commercial ask & success criteria: target NRR, rollout timeline, pilot acceptance tests.

Pricing guidance and worked examples

Redwood offers three commercial shapes: Hosted (pay-as-you-go + tiered volume discounts), Dedicated (monthly reserved GPU capacity), and Private (license + support). Guidance below is illustrative — use current pricing matrix from Commercial before committing.

Assumptions used in examples: average tokens per request = 400, concurrent QPS = 20, 30-day month.

Example A — Hosted (low-lift pilot)
- Base published rate: $0.0007 per input token, $0.0010 per output token (example public list prices).
- Monthly token volume: 400 tokens * 20 QPS * 3600 * 24 * 30 = ~691M tokens.
- Estimated monthly cost: (691M * ($0.0007 + $0.0010)) ≈ $1.17M.
- Suggested pilot discount: 30% off for first 90 days with 30-day termination.

Example B — Dedicated (predictable throughput)
- Typical small dedicated pool: 8x A100-equivalent GPUs with reserved throughput for 20 QPS at 512-token workloads.
- Committed monthly spend (example): $65k–$95k depending on instance mix and support tier.
- Notes: Reserved capacity reduces per-token costs by 50–70% vs unreserved Hosted at scale due to packing and quantized kernels.

Example C — Private (on-prem / VPC)
- Commercial structure: one-time platform license + annual support + optional on-prem packaging/airgap.
- Typical first-year total (mid-market): $350k–$1.2M depending on hardware, installation, and integration services.

Pricing negotiation levers to offer

- Pilot discounts, time-limited credits, and no-charge ingress networking for first 90 days.
- Committed reserved capacity vs volume discounts on Hosted.
- Optional Professional Services block for model onboarding and rollout testing (discounted for larger contracts).

Two concise case summaries (for slide use)

1) Retail search company (Platform improvement, mid-market)
- Situation: interactive product search with 120ms target p95 and unpredictable token volumes during campaigns.
- What we delivered: Dedicated pool + prefix caching and smart routing to cheaper quantized variants for background rerank jobs.
- Outcome: p95 improved from 340ms (prior vendor) to 180ms, monthly inference spend down 38% after traffic re-routing and cache tuning.

2) Healthcare analytics (Regulated, enterprise)
- Situation: strict PHI handling, on-prem requirement with ksyms in HSM, and audited access controls.
- What we delivered: Private deployment (air-gapped), KMS/HSM integration, 90-day audit report and quarterly security reviews.
- Outcome: Successful SOC2-aligned audit, 0 production incidents in first 12 months, and onboarding time reduced by 40% due to our deployment templates.

Security FAQ (top questions from CTOs/security leads)

Q: How do you protect customer keys and secrets?
A: Customer keys can be managed via customer-managed KMS. For Private we support HSM-backed key stores and strict separation of control plane credentials.

Q: What audit evidence do you provide?
A: Per-route access logs, request/response hashes (configurable retention), deployment change logs, and role-based access reports for the last 90/365 days.

Q: Can we run Redwood completely air-gapped?
A: Yes. We offer an on-prem air-gapped package with discrete install artifacts, offline license activation, and a hardened control plane option.

Q: How do you ensure model lineage and versioning?
A: Models are versioned in our catalog with immutable artifacts, signed manifests, and rollout metadata that supports canary and A/B policies.

Q: What are typical compliance artifacts you can share?
A: SOC2 readiness pack, network diagrams, pen-test summaries (redacted), and deployment checklists. We can provide a tailored compliance annex during procurement.

Pilot acceptance checklist (technical)

1) Performance: p95 latency for target request size <= agreed pilot p95.
2) Cost telemetry: token-level cost breakdown visible in Console for all pilot routes.
3) Observability: tracing across request path and KV cache hit-rate exposed.
4) Security: KMS integration and audit logs enabled for pilot tenants.
5) Rollout: ability to pin production route to pilot model and perform immediate fallback in case of regression.

Commercial ask template (one-liner to close on call)

"If we can sign a 90-day pilot with a 30% pilot credit and a technical success criteria of [pilot checklist], can we get procurement terms started today so we can begin onboarding next week?"

Recommended collateral (leave-behinds)

- One-page architecture diagram customized to prospect environment.
- Pilot runbook with acceptance criteria and schedule.
- Pricing scenario spreadsheet (editable) with token assumptions.
- Security annex (redacted SOC2 pack + deployment checklist).

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner (pre-sales): Senior Solutions Engineer (SE) assigned to opportunity.
- Commercial owner: Account Executive.
- Technical escalation: Platform field engineering + runtime team on standby for Dedicated/Private installs.

Appendix (configs, SLO examples, sample clauses)

- Example SLOs: "Regional Dedicated pool: 99.9% uptime; p95 <= 220ms for 512-token gen; error rate < 0.1% over 24h window."
- Example contract clause (data residency): "All inference request payloads and logs for customer X will be stored in region Y and will be retained for no longer than 90 days unless otherwise specified in writing."

Next steps (playbook for the AE/SE)

1) Pre-call prep: confirm prospect scale metrics, ask for network diagrams, and request a sample prompt set for eval.
2) Technical discovery (90 min): validate QPS, SLO targets, compliance needs, and failover scenarios.
3) Pilot proposal: deliver pilot runbook + pricing scenario within 3 business days of discovery.
4) Pilot kickoff: 2–4 week pilot with weekly syncs and final acceptance test at end.
